To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the UK's current approach to household energy use is founded upon a methodological individualism which assumes that greater provision of information will lead to behaviour change; 2) this approach is potentially limited, as it does not afford recognition to all those impacted by energy policy; 3) a community knowledge networks (CKN) approach to household energy offers an alternative perspective that recognises the contexts in which energy practices occur, but also offers a means for greater recognitional justice.

community knowledge networks can help to provide greater recognition of energy practices in the community, and that this approach can help to provide the basis for more just and equitable energy policies.

a community knowledge networks (CKN) approach to energy research and practice offers a more effective way of engaging with the energy justice agenda, as it recognises the situated nature of energy use, the importance of context and relationships, and the need to recognise the diversity of social groups affected by energy policy, and to provide appropriate forms of recognitional justice.
